reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / ATS-IDSA NTM guidance
clinicalPearls: A slow-growing non-chromogenic mycobacterium that can take several weeks to grow, so prolonged incubation is important
Shows striking geographical clustering, being reported particularly from northern Europe, including Scandinavia and the United Kingdom
Acquired from the environment (soil and water), it most often causes chronic pulmonary disease resembling that due to Mycobacterium avium complex or M. kansasii
Typically affects middle-aged and older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pneumoconiosis, or a smoking history, producing cavitary or fibronodular changes
In young children it is a recognised cause of cervical lymphadenitis
Its slow growth means cultures may be reported as negative if not held long enough
Treatment is with rifampicin and ethambutol, often with a macrolide or a quinolone, while childhood lymphadenitis is managed by surgical excision
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium malmoense is a slow-growing, non-pigmented environmental mycobacterium found in soil and water, with a distinct geographical distribution favouring northern Europe. Inhalation causes pulmonary infection chiefly in adults with pre-existing lung damage, producing a granulomatous, often cavitating process similar to that of M. avium complex and M. kansasii. In immunocompetent children the organism localises to cervical lymph nodes, as with other nontuberculous mycobacteria. Its very slow growth in culture can delay or prevent diagnosis unless incubation is sufficiently prolonged.
additionalDifferentials: Mycobacterium avium complex or M. kansasii lung disease
Other cavitary NTM lung disease (M. xenopi)
Nontuberculous mycobacterial or tuberculous lymphadenitis in children
additionalInvestigations: Mycobacterial culture with prolonged incubation given slow growth
Chest radiograph and CT for cavitary or fibronodular disease
Repeated respiratory cultures to satisfy diagnostic criteria
Excisional biopsy and culture for suspected childhood lymphadenitis
Assessment of underlying lung disease and immune status
redFlags: Progressive cavitary disease with constitutional symptoms or haemoptysis
Facial-nerve proximity when excising cervical nodes in children
Prolonged culture-negative results despite strong clinical suspicion
reference.prognosis: Pulmonary disease responds reasonably to prolonged rifampicin- and ethambutol-based combination therapy, though relapse can occur and outcomes are influenced by underlying lung disease. Childhood cervical lymphadenitis does well after complete surgical excision.
pitfalls: Discarding cultures before slow growth can be detected
Failing to meet diagnostic criteria before treating respiratory isolates
Performing incision and drainage of a child's node, promoting a chronic sinus
Assuming the same regimen and response as for M. tuberculosis
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
ATS/IDSA guideline on nontuberculous mycobacterial diseases
management: Treat pulmonary disease with prolonged rifampicin- and ethambutol-based combination therapy, commonly with the addition of a macrolide such as clarithromycin
Ensure sufficiently prolonged culture incubation to confirm the diagnosis, since this very slow grower may otherwise be reported as negative
Manage the underlying lung disease, such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and support smoking cessation
Monitor treatment response with repeated respiratory cultures and watch for drug toxicity, including ethambutol-related visual changes
Treat childhood cervical lymphadenitis with complete surgical excision
Refer to infectious diseases or respiratory medicine, recognising that relapse can occur and outcomes are shaped by underlying lung disease
